themes.label: Direct calls to political action (contact legislators, vote, mobilize)
defining_features: call_to_action (urges audience to lobby Congress / join supporting a cause)
call_to_action (explicit vote instruction; vote blue / vote for named candidate)
call_to_action (imperatives like BUILD THE BORDER WALL, Action now)
call_to_action (concrete agenda steps like releasing documents)
themes.interpretation: Posts that end with explicit mobilization (vote, lobby, join, act now) are a prominent moderation-relevant signal; in this corpus they appear more often in keep than remove.

themes.label: Policy-domain disputes (guns/gun laws, climate policy/tariffs, abortion/reproductive rights, immigration/DACA)
defining_features: primary_policy_domain includes guns/gun laws/Second Amendment/assault weapons
primary_policy_domain includes climate policy/carbon tariffs/affordability impacts
primary_policy_domain includes abortion/reproductive freedoms
specific_policy_domain includes immigration/DACA/Dream Act
themes.interpretation: A core theme is substantive political issue framing; moderation may need to distinguish issue debate (often kept) from escalated hostile language targeting people.

themes.label: Dehumanizing/abusive or highly aggressive insults (profanity, slurs, extreme labels)
defining_features: profanity_or_taboo_language (explicit profanity or taboo insults; sexualized or violent taboo labels)
dehumanizing_or_extreme_insulting_language (filth/rot/sewer metaphors)
ridicule_or_mockery (dismissive/derisive labeling like moron/fascist in chief)
high_punctuation_intensity (maximal insult piling with intense punctuation)
themes.interpretation: This is the strongest moderation-relevant pattern: explicit profanity and dehumanizing/extreme abuse correlate heavily with remove outcomes in the corpus.

themes.label: Us-vs-them / blame assignment to political groups (outgroup labels, scapegoating, bloc contrast)
defining_features: us_vs_them_framing (ingroup/outgroup competence or ideology contrast; rich vs little guy)
target_directionality (assigns blame to named party: Democrats/Republicans, MAGA vs others)
elite_vs_populist_framing (oligarchs manipulating/cheating outcomes)
us_vs_them_framing includes shifting blame away from scapegoats (e.g., immigrants) toward elites
themes.interpretation: Group-based antagonism and blame targeting appear in both labels; risk likely increases when combined with abusive language and/or conspiratorial certainty.

themes.label: Conspiracy or manipulation framing (deep state, psyop, systemic corruption built-in, election theft)
defining_features: conspiratorial_framing (deep state/media convinced them)
conspiratorial_framing (climate crisis as manufactured psyop)
conspiratorial_framing (corruption/overreach built into the system)
conspiratorial_framing (election theft 'so significant and complete')
themes.interpretation: Conspiracy/mistrust narratives are more often associated with remove ratings, suggesting a moderation concern with claims that imply deception or undemocratic wrongdoing without substantiation.

themes.label: Moral or religious valuation and moral condemnation (pro-life, “monster,” disgust framing)
defining_features: normative_moral_language (religious framing; pro-life absolute moral claims)
normative_moral_language (moralized disgust/ethical condemnation)
ridicule_or_mockery (moral shaming like 'You're a monster')
positive_evaluation_and_propagandistic_language (endorse agreement as 'step in the right direction')
themes.interpretation: Morality-based framing appears more in keep than remove here, indicating that moral argumentation itself is not necessarily the primary risk; escalation depends on hostility/profanity.

themes.label: Factual assertion vs speculation; numeric/empirical support
defining_features: factual_assertion_vs_speculation (legal/process facts; cause-effect interpretations)
economic_cost_benefit_framing (relative prices, money-flow claims)
factual_assertion_vs_speculation includes percentage/statistic evidence
economic_cost_benefit_framing includes affordability/wages/leave money-flow
themes.interpretation: Posts using empirical-sounding claims, legal/process details, and quantified comparisons tend to be kept more often, suggesting moderation favors substance over purely hostile insinuation.

themes.label: Quoting/attribution and mirroring argument structure (direct quotes; 'I mean' pivots; mirror shifts blame)
defining_features: quote_or_attribution_embedding (multiple direct quotes from named persons/poems)
contrastive_but_however_structure (I mean pivot; however clauses)
mirror_shift_direction (re-target blame or moral framing via mirror)
list_or_enumeration (structured bullet lists of policy items)
themes.interpretation: Compositional argument techniques (quoting, pivots, mirror framing, enumeration) are present mainly in kept posts; they may help distinguish structured argumentation from raw abusive rants.

themes.label: Escalatory threat/urgent catastrophe framing (apocalyptic decline, existential threats, “unless…” consequences)
defining_features: emphatic_outrage (apocalyptic/rapid decline warnings if not removed)
victimhood_or_persecution_framing (existential threat to group; collective harm if democracy lost)
conditional_if_then_structure (If you… then catastrophe / if we lose… we’re all fucked)
themes.interpretation: Catastrophic or existential threat framing occurs but is less frequent in keep; when it appears alongside other aggravating features it likely contributes to removal.

cross_cutting_themes: Aggressive language escalation: when profanity/dehumanization (Theme 3) combines with group blame (Theme 4) or conspiracy certainty (Theme 5), removals increase markedly.
Issue debate vs personal hostility: the same policy domains (Theme 2) can be expressed with empirical/legal support (Theme 7, keep-leaning) or with extreme abuse (Theme 3, remove-leaning).
Persuasive structure without abuse: quoting/pivots/mirrors and enumerated arguments (Theme 8) often coexist with factual/empirical framing (Theme 7) in keep-rated posts.
Mobilization and political advocacy: calls to action (Theme 1) are common and mostly compatible with non-abusive, structured argumentation (Themes 7–8).
